anti_patterns.description: `const data = await response.json()` used directly in components without Zod validation — API shape changes cause silent runtime errors instead of caught schema validation failures.

standards.title: Angular Validators on All API Responses — Angular Stack
standards.statement: Angular services validate API responses using TypeScript interfaces with runtime type guards before passing data to components. Pydantic models on the FastAPI side and TypeScript interfaces on the Angular side maintain schema parity. Any response that fails validation is treated as an error and handled via the error state, not silently consumed.

anti_patterns.description: Casting API responses with `as SomeType` without runtime validation — TypeScript type assertions do not validate data at runtime; a schema change produces a runtime error in production.

standards.title: No `console.log` in Production — Sentry for Error Tracking
standards.statement: `console.log`, `console.error`, and `console.warn` are forbidden in production code. Errors and unexpected states are reported to Sentry via the frontend error boundary. Development-only logging uses an environment-gated logger utility that no-ops in production.

anti_patterns.description: `console.error(error)` as the catch block in an API call — the error is swallowed; no alert is triggered; no error tracking captures it.

standards.title: TanStack Query for Server State — Next.js Stack
standards.statement: TanStack Query (React Query) manages all server state in Next.js applications. Server state (API data, remote data) is never managed with `useState` + `useEffect` combinations. TanStack Query provides caching, background refetching, loading/error states, and mutation tracking — all concerns that `useState` + `useEffect` patterns implement incorrectly.

anti_patterns.description: `const [data, setData] = useState(null); useEffect(() => { fetch(url).then(r => r.json()).then(setData) }, [])` — no loading state, no error state, no caching, no refetch on window focus, stale data on navigation.

standards.title: Zustand for Client State — Next.js Stack
standards.statement: Zustand manages client-side application state (UI state, modal open/close, filter selections, wizard step, user preferences). Redux is not used. Context API is used only for dependency injection (themes, i18n) — not for state management. The separation between server state (TanStack Query) and client state (Zustand) is maintained strictly.

anti_patterns.description: Caching API responses in Zustand alongside UI state — duplicates TanStack Query's cache management without its invalidation, deduplication, or background refetch capabilities.

standards.title: Angular Signals for Reactive State — Angular Stack
standards.statement: Angular Signals are the primary state management tool for all new Angular code. RxJS Observables are used for HTTP requests, WebSocket streams, and complex async compositions. BehaviorSubject is used only where signals cannot serve the use case. NgRx is not introduced unless the system complexity specifically justifies it, documented in an ADR.

anti_patterns.description: Using BehaviorSubject for simple local component state that a Signal handles more cleanly — over-engineering that makes the state harder to reason about.

standards.title: Zustand and Signal Stores Are Flat — No Nested State Trees
standards.statement: Client state stores are flat — no deeply nested state objects. Nested state requires nested update logic that is error-prone. If state naturally nests, separate it into distinct stores or signals with explicit cross-references.

anti_patterns.description: A single Zustand store with `user.preferences.notifications.email.daily` depth — immutable update of deeply nested state is complex and error-prone.

standards.title: No Prop Drilling Beyond Two Levels — Context or State Store
standards.statement: Props that need to pass through more than two component levels are moved to a context provider or state store. Prop drilling beyond two levels creates implicit coupling between components that should have no dependency on each other's data needs.

anti_patterns.description: Passing `currentUser` through five component levels when a Zustand store makes it directly available — every intermediate component takes a dependency on a prop it doesn't use.

standards.title: API error responses are always surfaced to the user with an actionable message
standards.statement: API error responses are always surfaced to the user with an actionable message — never silently swallowed. Error messages use plain language: "Could not load applications — try again" not "Error 500."

standards.title: Optimistic updates include rollback logic
standards.statement: Optimistic updates include rollback logic — if the API call fails, the UI reverts to its pre-update state and displays an error.

standards.title: Data fetched for display is never mutated directly
standards.statement: Data fetched for display is never mutated directly — TanStack Query invalidation or Signal derivation produces new values; mutation of cache data directly is forbidden.

standards.title: Infinite scroll and paginated lists use cursor-based pagination (aligned with…
standards.statement: Infinite scroll and paginated lists use cursor-based pagination (aligned with S2.39) — offset pagination breaks when items are added or removed between pages.

standards.title: Local state that does not need to survive page navigation is component-scoped,…
standards.statement: Local state that does not need to survive page navigation is component-scoped, not store-scoped — not everything belongs in a global store.

standards.title: WebSocket connections are managed in services (Angular) or custom hooks…
standards.statement: WebSocket connections are managed in services (Angular) or custom hooks (Next.js), not in components — components subscribe to the stream, they do not own the connection.

standards.title: Derived state is computed, not stored
standards.statement: Derived state is computed, not stored — if a value can be derived from existing state, it is a computed value, not a stored value.

standards.title: Real-time feature state falls back to polling on WebSocket disconnect
standards.statement: Real-time feature state falls back to polling on WebSocket disconnect — fallback prevents silent data staleness.

standards.title: Forms are not server state
standards.statement: Forms are not server state — form inputs and draft state live in local component state or form libraries, not in TanStack Query or global stores.

standards.title: Feature flag state is read from the database via API on session start
standards.statement: Feature flag state is read from the database via API on session start — never hardcoded in frontend code.

standards.title: Dark mode preference is stored in localStorage and applied before first paint
standards.statement: Dark mode preference is stored in localStorage and applied before first paint — prevents flash of wrong theme.

standards.title: URL state (filters, pagination, sort) is encoded in query parameters
standards.statement: URL state (filters, pagination, sort) is encoded in query parameters — enables deep linking and browser back/forward navigation to work correctly.

standards.title: State resets on route navigation unless explicitly preserved
standards.statement: State resets on route navigation unless explicitly preserved — stale state from a previous route contaminating a new route is a code review block.

standards.title: React Hook Form + Zod for All Forms — Next.js Stack
standards.statement: All forms use React Hook Form with Zod for validation. Uncontrolled form state management with `useState` per field is forbidden. Zod schemas define validation rules and TypeScript types simultaneously — the schema is the single source of truth for form shape.

anti_patterns.description: `const [email, setEmail] = useState("")` for every form field individually — uncontrolled form state management that does not provide validation, error state, or submit handling.

standards.title: Angular Reactive Forms for All Forms — Angular Stack
standards.statement: All Angular forms use Reactive Forms (`FormBuilder`, `FormGroup`, `FormControl`). Template-driven forms are forbidden. Reactive Forms are testable, provide synchronous validation, and enable complex validation patterns. Form state is managed by the `FormGroup` — not by component properties.

anti_patterns.description: `[(ngModel)]` two-way binding for form inputs — template-driven forms are untestable without full component rendering and cannot express complex cross-field validation.

standards.title: Client-Side Validation Is UX — Server-Side Is Authoritative
standards.statement: Client-side form validation provides immediate user feedback (UX). Server-side validation is the authoritative gate. Every form submission is validated on the server — client-side validation is never the security or data integrity layer.

anti_patterns.description: Removing a required field from the Zod schema without updating the Pydantic model — client no longer validates the field but the server still rejects it; or vice versa, creating a gap.

standards.title: Form errors display inline, adjacent to the field that caused them
standards.statement: Form errors display inline, adjacent to the field that caused them — not as a modal or toast. Toast is reserved for async operation feedback (save success, delete confirmation), not form validation.

standards.title: Multi-step forms preserve completed step data on back navigation
standards.statement: Multi-step forms preserve completed step data on back navigation — users never lose work by clicking back.

standards.title: Form submission disables the submit button and shows a loading indicator during…
standards.statement: Form submission disables the submit button and shows a loading indicator during the API call — prevents double-submission.

standards.title: Standalone Components — Preferred Over NgModules
standards.statement: All new Angular components, directives, and pipes use the `standalone: true` pattern. NgModules are used only for third-party library integration that requires module-based bootstrapping. Standalone components have explicit imports and are independently testable.

anti_patterns.description: Creating a new NgModule to organise a feature when a standalone component with explicit imports achieves the same result — NgModules add indirection without benefit in modern Angular.

standards.title: OnPush Change Detection — All Components
standards.statement: All Angular components use `ChangeDetectionStrategy.OnPush`. Default change detection is forbidden in production Angular code. OnPush components only re-render when their input references change, an async pipe emits, or a Signal changes — this is a prerequisite for performant Angular applications.

anti_patterns.description: `ChangeDetectionStrategy.Default` on components — Angular re-checks every component on every event, creating performance degradation at scale.

standards.title: Angular Route Guards — UX Protection Only (Server Is Authoritative)

depends_on.description: C3 — route guards are UX only

standards.statement: Angular route guards redirect unauthenticated users to the login page for UX purposes. They are not the authorisation mechanism. The FastAPI `Depends()` layer is the authoritative security gate. See S3.19 for the security rationale.

anti_patterns.description: Treating route guard bypass as a security incident — the server-side auth prevented data access; the route guard only prevented the Angular navigation.

cross_references.description: C3 Auth — route guards are UX

standards.title: Angular Services for All API Calls and State — No Direct HTTP in Components
standards.statement: All API calls, state management, and business logic live in injectable Angular services. Components inject services and subscribe to their outputs. Direct `HttpClient` calls inside components are forbidden. This makes components testable without mocking HTTP.

anti_patterns.description: `this.http.get('/api/students')` inside an Angular component constructor — the component cannot be unit-tested without a mock HTTP backend.

standards.title: Vitest for Angular Unit Tests — Never Karma or Jasmine
standards.statement: Angular unit tests use Vitest with `@analogjs/vitest-angular`. Karma and Jasmine are not installed or used. Playwright handles E2E and visual regression. This aligns the Angular testing toolchain with the Next.js testing approach (both use Vite-compatible tooling).

anti_patterns.description: Keeping Karma in `angular.json` alongside Vitest — dual test runner configurations produce inconsistent results and CI complexity.

standards.title: The `async` pipe is used in templates to subscribe to Observables
standards.statement: The `async` pipe is used in templates to subscribe to Observables — manual subscriptions in `ngOnInit` that are not unsubscribed are a memory leak.

standards.title: Angular CLI generates all components, services, and guards
standards.statement: Angular CLI generates all components, services, and guards — no hand-crafted Angular boilerplate.

standards.title: Environment files (`environment.ts`, `environment.prod.ts`) reference only…
standards.statement: Environment files (`environment.ts`, `environment.prod.ts`) reference only variable names, not values — actual values come from Railway Secrets via build configuration.

standards.title: `ngFor` always uses a `trackBy` function
standards.statement: `ngFor` always uses a `trackBy` function — prevents full re-render of list items on data update.

standards.title: shadcn/ui for Next.js Component Library — No Custom Primitives from Scratch
standards.statement: shadcn/ui is the Next.js component library. Buttons, forms, dialogs, dropdowns, and tables use shadcn/ui as the base. Custom components extend or compose shadcn/ui primitives. Building accessible, keyboard-navigable UI primitives from scratch in v1 is not justified when shadcn/ui provides them correctly.

anti_patterns.description: Building a custom accessible Modal component for v1 when shadcn/ui's `<Dialog>` already implements the ARIA dialog pattern correctly.

standards.title: Admin dashboards are Group 3 features
standards.statement: Admin dashboards are Group 3 features — not built before the primary user workflow is complete and shipped.

standards.title: Animation libraries (Framer Motion, GSAP) are deferred to v2 unless the…
standards.statement: Animation libraries (Framer Motion, GSAP) are deferred to v2 unless the animation is core to the primary user workflow — no animation in v1 that is not directly tied to a user-facing functional interaction.

standards.title: Frontend internationalisation (i18n) is not implemented in v1 for any system
standards.statement: Frontend internationalisation (i18n) is not implemented in v1 for any system — the user base is English-speaking South African users; i18n is a v2 feature when the user base has been confirmed.

standards.title: Sentry Frontend Integration — Error Capture and User Context
standards.statement: Sentry is initialised in every frontend application with: DSN from environment variable, release version from build metadata, user context set on authentication (id, role — never email or PII beyond what Sentry's PII scrubbing can handle), and environment tag (development/staging/production). Every unhandled Promise rejection and React/Angular error boundary catch is sent to Sentry.

anti_patterns.description: Sentry `console.error` integration without explicit user context — errors arrive in Sentry with no way to identify affected users or correlate with backend errors from the same session.

standards.title: Error Boundaries on Every Route and Async Feature Area
standards.statement: React error boundaries wrap every page/route and every major async feature area in Next.js. Angular's global error handler and component-level error handling cover Angular systems. An uncaught render error must not take down the entire application — it shows an error UI for that section only.

anti_patterns.description: No error boundary around the dashboard feature area — an error in one widget unmounts the entire dashboard.

standards.title: Vercel Analytics is enabled on all Next.js deployments
standards.statement: Vercel Analytics is enabled on all Next.js deployments — Core Web Vitals (LCP, CLS, FID) are tracked per deployment and reviewed post-deploy.

standards.title: `X-Request-ID` header is attached to every frontend API call
standards.statement: `X-Request-ID` header is attached to every frontend API call — enables correlation between frontend Sentry errors and backend log entries for the same request.

standards.title: Performance budget: Lighthouse performance score ≥ 80 on mobile in CI
standards.statement: Performance budget: Lighthouse performance score ≥ 80 on mobile in CI — a score below 80 is a build warning, below 70 is a build failure.

standards.title: Real-time features log connection and disconnection events to Sentry with user…
standards.statement: Real-time features log connection and disconnection events to Sentry with user context — enables diagnosing WebSocket reliability issues in production.

standards.title: Feature Groups Define Build Sequence Within Each Sprint
standards.statement: Within each sprint, frontend features are built in group order: Group 1 (core primary workflow) → Group 2 (supporting primary workflow) → Group 3 (secondary features). No Group 3 feature begins before Group 1 and 2 features for that sprint are complete and merged. Group ordering within the frontend build sequence follows the same logic as the platform-level group ordering in C9.

anti_patterns.description: Building the admin dashboard (Group 3) before the primary submission form (Group 1) is complete — when Group 1 encounters a blocking issue, Group 3 work is wasted.

standards.title: Each feature group has one designated owner who signs off on the group's…
standards.statement: Each feature group has one designated owner who signs off on the group's completion before the next group begins.

standards.title: Group completion criteria
standards.statement: Group completion criteria: all standards pass, all tests pass, CI green, PR merged to main, preview deployment functional.

standards.title: Group 1 features ship before any Group 2 feature is started within the same…
standards.statement: Group 1 features ship before any Group 2 feature is started within the same sprint.

standards.title: Cross-group dependencies are documented in the feature proposal
standards.statement: Cross-group dependencies are documented in the feature proposal — if Group 2 depends on Group 1 data, this is explicit and tracked.

standards.title: A group that slips (incomplete at sprint end) is moved to the next sprint as…
standards.statement: A group that slips (incomplete at sprint end) is moved to the next sprint as Group 1 priority — partial groups are never shipped.

standards.title: Group retrospective
standards.statement: Group retrospective: after each group ships, 30 minutes reviewing what the group revealed about the next group's requirements — not a process ceremony, a design input.

standards.title: Group build history is tracked in the system context file…
standards.statement: Group build history is tracked in the system context file (`system-contexts/{system}-context.md`) — current group, completed groups, next group, open issues per group.

standards.title: Layer Build Order: Interface → Service → Component → UI
standards.statement: Every frontend feature is built in this exact layer order: (1) **Interface/Types** — TypeScript interfaces, Zod schemas, Angular service interfaces. (2) **Service layer** — Angular services or Next.js API client functions that communicate with the backend. (3) **Smart component** — the container that calls services and manages state. (4) **UI/Presentational components** — pure rendering components that receive data via props/inputs. Each layer is committed separately before the next begins.
standards.rationale: Building in layer order forces the interface contract to be defined before implementation. It prevents the common failure of building UI and then discovering the data shape doesn't fit. It produces a commit history that documents how the feature was assembled, making code review and debugging dramatically more tractable.

anti_patterns.description: Building the UI component first and working backwards to the API — the UI shape drives the API shape, reversing the contract-first principle.
One giant commit containing all four layers — layers cannot be reviewed independently; the build history is opaque.

standards.title: One Commit Per Layer — Not One Commit Per Feature
standards.statement: The commit log for a feature contains four commits minimum: one per layer from S4.79. Commits use conventional commit format. Each commit is pushed before the next layer begins. This is not bureaucratic process — it is the discipline that makes rollbacks layer-precise and code review layer-scoped.
standards.rationale: A single `feat: add scholarship application form` commit containing 800 lines of changes across all layers cannot be meaningfully reviewed. Four layer-scoped commits of 200 lines each can be reviewed with precision. If the UI layer is wrong, only that commit needs revision.

anti_patterns.description: `git add . && git commit -m "feat: application form"` after completing all four layers — unreviewed layer mixing; makes rollback impossible at the layer level.

standards.title: TypeScript interfaces and Zod schemas defined in the first layer commit are…
standards.statement: TypeScript interfaces and Zod schemas defined in the first layer commit are never changed without updating the service and component layers in the same PR — interface changes cascade downward, never upward.

standards.title: The layer build order applies to bug fixes as well as features
standards.statement: The layer build order applies to bug fixes as well as features — a bug fix that touches all four layers follows the same layer sequence in separate commits.

standards.title: The Frontend Is Fully Designed and Ratified Before the Build Session
enforced_by: Founder ratification before the build session
standards.statement: Before a frontend build session begins, the system's frontend is fully DESIGNED and Founder-ratified as a documented design package, covering: the workspace file/folder structure; the design tokens (semantic colour for light AND dark, type scale, spacing, motion) with an explicit accessibility + performance budget (WCAG 2.2 AA, Core Web Vitals targets); the component library (the four states, forms, tables, overlays); navigation and the layout shells; the marketing/public surface (if any); and a build-ready design handoff that names the read order and the contracts the UI must honour. The build session EXECUTES the design — it does not invent it. The design package lives in a discoverable docs location (e.g. `docs/experience/`) and is referenced by the stage brief. A build that begins without a ratified design package is stopped at review.
standards.rationale: A frontend invented commit-by-commit accrues design debt: inconsistent spacing and colour, retrofitted accessibility, a navigation that fights itself, and rework when the look is finally "decided" after it is built. Designing the whole surface first — tokens, components, navigation, the budget — makes the build a translation of a ratified, coherent, accessible, premium design rather than a series of local guesses. Design is the cheapest place to get the experience right; code is the most expensive.

anti_patterns.description: A frontend build session started with no ratified design package — tokens, components, and navigation are improvised in code; the result is inconsistent and accrues design debt and rework.

cross_references.description: layer build order — the build follows the design
the styling philosophy the tokens implement

standards.title: Three-Database Separation — One Purpose Per Database Type

depends_on.description: stack assignment determines which databases are used

standards.statement: Three database technologies serve three purposes. PostgreSQL: structured relational data, ACID guarantees, all entities with relationships or financial implications. MongoDB: flexible document data, schema-evolving content, AI-generated content, application logs — Angular stack only. ChromaDB: vector embeddings, semantic similarity search, RAG context — FundsLink Academy only. A data entity that belongs to one type must never be stored in another.
standards.rationale: The most expensive production database mistake is putting financial data in a non-ACID store, or putting schema-evolving content in a rigid relational schema. The three-database separation is designed to prevent both errors by making the assignment criteria explicit before schema work begins.

anti_patterns.description: Storing financial transaction amounts in MongoDB because "it's already there" — MongoDB's eventual consistency model provides no ACID guarantees; balance inconsistency becomes possible.
Storing vector embeddings in PostgreSQL `JSONB` columns — PostgreSQL is not a vector similarity database; cosine similarity over JSONB is orders of magnitude slower than ChromaDB.

standards.title: PostgreSQL Is the System of Record — All Entities Originate Here
standards.statement: Every core entity — user, student, funder, resident, account holder, creator — is first created and owned by PostgreSQL. MongoDB documents and ChromaDB embeddings reference these entities but are subordinate. If PostgreSQL and MongoDB ever report conflicting state for the same entity, PostgreSQL is correct. MongoDB is updated to match PostgreSQL.
standards.rationale: Without a designated system of record, conflicts between databases have no resolution authority. The PostgreSQL-as-primary rule eliminates this ambiguity — there is always one source of truth for entity identity.

anti_patterns.description: Creating a user document in MongoDB before creating the corresponding User record in PostgreSQL — the MongoDB document references an entity that does not yet exist.

standards.title: Financial Data in PostgreSQL Only — Never MongoDB or Redis
standards.statement: All financial data — account balances, transaction amounts, deposit schedules, interest rates, lock periods, payment records — must live exclusively in PostgreSQL. This rule has no exceptions. MongoDB's eventual consistency and lack of native multi-document ACID transactions make it structurally unsuitable for financial records. Redis without persistence cannot guarantee durability.
standards.rationale: A balance inconsistency caused by non-ACID storage is a financial integrity failure. Reserve Bank deposit schedules, FundsLink funding amounts, and any monetary calculation that must be correct for regulatory and user trust reasons require the full ACID guarantees only PostgreSQL provides.

anti_patterns.description: `deposits_collection` in MongoDB with `amount` and `balance` fields — this is the CF-03 failure; MongoDB's lack of ACID means partial writes can leave balances inconsistent.

standards.title: Authentication Data in PostgreSQL Only

depends_on.description: C3 Auth — mandates PostgreSQL for auth data

standards.statement: All authentication data — user credentials, password hashes, JWT refresh tokens, reset tokens, email verification tokens, session records, role assignments — lives in PostgreSQL. Authentication requires ACID consistency to prevent race conditions in token validation and session management. See S3.2 for the security rationale.

anti_patterns.description: Session table in MongoDB on the Angular stack — MongoDB's eventual consistency creates race conditions in session invalidation, allowing revoked sessions to remain valid briefly.

standards.title: Cross-Database References Use PostgreSQL `cuid` — Never MongoDB ObjectID
standards.statement: When a MongoDB document or ChromaDB embedding references an entity that exists in PostgreSQL, the reference field stores the PostgreSQL `cuid` string value. MongoDB ObjectIDs are never used as cross-database foreign references. This keeps PostgreSQL as the unambiguous system of record and enables joins at the application layer without ambiguity.

anti_patterns.description: `student_id: ObjectId` in a MongoDB scholarship document — MongoDB ObjectID has no meaning in PostgreSQL; the application layer cannot resolve the reference without a MongoDB query first.

standards.title: Database Selection Documented at Design Time — Never at Implementation Time
standards.statement: Every new data entity has its database destination documented in the feature proposal before schema work begins. The proposal must answer: relational joins needed? ACID required? Schema fixed or dynamic? AI-generated content? The answers determine the database. No ad-hoc database decisions at implementation time.

anti_patterns.description: "We'll figure out where to store this when we build it" — ad-hoc decisions made at implementation time are driven by convenience rather than correctness.

cross_references.description: feature lifecycle — design phase includes database assignment

grounded_in: Coronel & Rob, *Database Systems* — Database Design (the database life cycle)

standards.title: No Direct Database Access from Frontend — Always Through Backend

depends_on.description: service layer owns all database access

standards.statement: The browser never connects directly to PostgreSQL, MongoDB, or ChromaDB. All database access goes through the backend service layer — Next.js API routes (Next.js stack) or FastAPI (Angular stack). No client-side Prisma client, no browser MongoDB driver, no direct ChromaDB HTTP calls from Angular.

anti_patterns.description: Prisma client imported in a Next.js client component — the database connection string is exposed to the browser bundle.

standards.title: Soft Delete on All Databases — Never Hard Delete in Production
standards.statement: No production record is ever permanently deleted by user action. PostgreSQL uses `deleted_at DateTime?` via Prisma. MongoDB uses `deletedAt: Date` via Beanie. ChromaDB documents are archived, not deleted. All queries default-filter records where `deleted_at IS NULL`. Hard deletes require a documented admin process and are never triggered by user-facing actions.
standards.rationale: Accidental deletions, disputes over deleted content, and audit requirements all require data to be recoverable. Hard deletes are irreversible; soft deletes are recoverable. The `deleted_at` filter is the default query behaviour, not an optional add-on.

anti_patterns.description: `prisma.user.delete()` called from a user-facing "Delete Account" endpoint — hard delete is irreversible; soft delete enables account recovery and audit.

standards.title: Prisma Schema Is the Single Source of Truth — All Changes Through Migrations
enforced_by: CI — `prisma migrate diff` on every schema PR
standards.statement: The Prisma schema file (`schema.prisma`) is the authoritative definition of all PostgreSQL tables, columns, indexes, and relations. All schema changes go through `prisma migrate dev` (development) or `prisma migrate deploy` (production). Manual SQL DDL (`CREATE TABLE`, `ALTER TABLE`, `DROP COLUMN`) is forbidden outside of migration files. Every migration file is reviewed in the PR that introduces it.
standards.rationale: Schema drift — where the database differs from what the application expects — is one of the most common causes of runtime errors. Prisma migrations maintain a complete history of every schema change and its order. Manual DDL bypasses this history, creating untracked drift.

anti_patterns.description: Running `ALTER TABLE users ADD COLUMN phone VARCHAR(20)` directly on the database — the schema change is not in version control, not reproducible, and unknown to other developers.
Editing `schema.prisma` without generating a migration — the schema and the database diverge silently until the next `prisma migrate status` reveals the drift.

standards.title: Required Fields on Every PostgreSQL Table
standards.statement: Every Prisma model must define four base fields: `id String @id @default(cuid())`, `created_at DateTime @default(now())`, `updated_at DateTime @updatedAt`, `deleted_at DateTime?`. A Prisma schema linter in CI fails the build if any model is missing these fields. The `cuid()` function is used for IDs — not `autoincrement()`, not `uuid()`.
standards.rationale: `cuid` IDs are safe to expose publicly (no sequential information), URL-safe, and sortable. The timestamp fields enable audit trails and time-based queries on every table. `deleted_at` enables soft delete across all models without per-model configuration.

anti_patterns.description: `id Int @id @default(autoincrement())` — sequential integer IDs expose the total record count and enable enumeration attacks.
A model without `deleted_at` — hard deletes become the only option when soft delete is needed later, requiring a migration.

grounded_in: Coronel & Rob, *Database Systems* — The Relational Database Model (entity integrity)

standards.title: No SELECT * — Explicit `select` on Every Prisma Query
standards.statement: Every `prisma.model.findMany()`, `findFirst()`, and `findUnique()` call includes an explicit `select` object listing only the fields required for that operation. Never call these methods without a `select` clause. This prevents accidental exposure of sensitive fields and reduces payload size.
standards.rationale: A `prisma.user.findMany()` without `select` returns `password_hash`, `reset_token`, `refresh_token`, and every other sensitive field to whatever code calls it. The API contract between the database and the service layer should be as narrow as the operation requires.

anti_patterns.description: `prisma.user.findMany()` without a `select` clause — returns all columns including password_hash, refresh tokens, and sensitive internal fields to the service layer.

standards.title: All Queries Filter `deleted_at: null` by Default
standards.statement: Every query on a soft-deletable model includes `where: { deleted_at: null }` unless explicitly fetching deleted records for admin purposes. A Prisma middleware automatically appends this filter to all queries, providing a safety net. Queries that intentionally include soft-deleted records document this explicitly with a comment.
standards.rationale: Without this filter, soft-deleted users can authenticate, soft-deleted scholarships appear in search results, and soft-deleted transactions appear in balance calculations. The middleware provides a system-level default; the standard requires explicit acknowledgement when the filter is intentionally bypassed.

anti_patterns.description: A balance calculation query that includes soft-deleted transactions — produces incorrect balance totals that inflate the calculated balance.

cross_references.description: raw SQL must also filter deleted_at

standards.title: Foreign Key Indexes on Every FK Field
standards.statement: Every foreign key field in the Prisma schema has an explicit `@@index` or `@index` annotation. Unindexed foreign keys cause full table scans on join queries. The Prisma schema linter in CI checks that all FK fields have indexes defined.

anti_patterns.description: `user_id String` in a Scholarship model without `@@index([user_id])` — every query filtering by `user_id` performs a full table scan as scholarship data grows.

grounded_in: Coronel & Rob, *Database Systems* — The Relational Database Model (referential integrity; indexes)

standards.title: Pagination on All List Queries — No Unbounded Results
standards.statement: Every Prisma query that returns a list of records includes `take` and `skip` (or cursor-based pagination). Default page size is 20 records. Maximum page size is 100 records. Never return an unbounded result set regardless of how few records currently exist. The `take` constraint is enforced at the Prisma query level — not by truncating an unbounded response.

anti_patterns.description: `prisma.scholarship.findMany({ where: { status: 'ACTIVE' } })` without `take` — works correctly with 50 scholarships, causes memory exhaustion with 50,000.

standards.title: Transactions for Multi-Step Writes — `prisma.$transaction()`
standards.statement: Any operation that writes to multiple tables must use `prisma.$transaction([])`. Never issue sequential writes without a transaction wrapper when partial failure would leave the database in an inconsistent state. This is especially critical for Reserve Bank deposit operations, FundsLink application submissions, role changes, and SyncUp pitch-to-subscription flows.
standards.rationale: Sequential writes without transactions create a window where write 1 succeeds and write 2 fails. The database is left in a partial state with no clean recovery path. `prisma.$transaction` ensures both succeed or both roll back.

anti_patterns.description: Sequential `prisma.deposit.create()` followed by `prisma.account.update()` without a transaction — a network error after the deposit creates an inconsistency where the deposit exists but the balance was not updated.

grounded_in: Coronel & Rob, *Database Systems* — Advanced SQL (transaction management)

standards.title: Prisma Singleton Client — Never Instantiate Per Request
standards.statement: The Prisma client is instantiated once as a singleton and imported from a shared module (`src/lib/prisma.ts` in Next.js). A new `PrismaClient()` is never instantiated per-request or per-function. Multiple client instances exhaust the PostgreSQL connection pool.

anti_patterns.description: `const prisma = new PrismaClient()` at the top of every API route file — each hot-reload or deployment creates new connections; the connection pool exhausts under normal traffic.

standards.title: Prisma Client Generates TypeScript Types — Never Cast or Override

depends_on.description: Prisma schema as source of truth

standards.statement: Prisma's generated TypeScript types are used throughout the service layer. Casting query results with `as SomeType` is forbidden when the Prisma-generated type is available. If a custom type is needed, it is derived from Prisma types using `Prisma.UserGetPayload<...>` utilities.

anti_patterns.description: `const user = (await prisma.user.findUnique(...)) as CustomUserType` — the TypeScript type assertion bypasses Prisma's type guarantees; schema changes cause runtime errors instead of compile-time errors.

standards.title: Beanie ODM for All MongoDB Access — Angular Stack
standards.statement: All MongoDB access on the Angular stack uses the Beanie ODM. Direct PyMongo collection access is used only when Beanie's API is insufficient for a specific operation, with a comment explaining why. Beanie provides Pydantic model validation, async support, and type safety at the MongoDB boundary — identical in philosophy to Prisma at the PostgreSQL boundary.

anti_patterns.description: `db["scholarship_content"].insert_one(doc)` without Beanie — bypasses Pydantic validation, loses type safety, and produces unvalidated data in MongoDB.

standards.title: Raw SQL for Complex Queries That ORM Cannot Express Cleanly
standards.statement: Raw SQL via `prisma.$queryRaw` (TypeScript) or `db.execute(text(...))` (Python/SQLAlchemy) is the correct tool for: complex aggregates with `GROUP BY` and `HAVING`, recursive CTEs for hierarchical data, window functions (`ROW_NUMBER`, `RANK`, `LAG`, `LEAD`), `LATERAL JOIN` patterns, reporting queries with complex filters, and precision financial calculations requiring SQL-native decimal arithmetic. Every raw SQL block must include a comment explaining why Prisma is insufficient for this specific query.
standards.rationale: Forcing complex aggregate or window function queries through an ORM produces either multiple round-trips to the database (N+1 patterns) or convoluted query builder chains that are harder to read than the equivalent SQL. The same logic that makes Tailwind insufficient for brand CSS makes ORM insufficient for complex analytics — the specialised tool is the right tool.

anti_patterns.description: Raw SQL for a simple `WHERE id = ? AND deleted_at IS NULL` query — Prisma handles this correctly and provides type safety; raw SQL adds no value and loses type checking.
Raw SQL without a comment explaining why ORM is insufficient — every raw SQL block in the codebase must justify its existence.

standards.title: Raw SQL Wrapped in Transactions for Multi-Step Operations
standards.statement: Raw SQL operations that involve multiple writes use `prisma.$transaction(async (tx) => { ... })` for interactive transactions, or explicit `BEGIN / COMMIT / ROLLBACK` when Prisma's transaction API is insufficient. Raw SQL writes that are not wrapped in a transaction are a code review block.
standards.rationale: The transaction requirement applies equally to ORM writes and raw SQL writes. The tool changes but the atomicity requirement does not. Multi-step raw SQL writes without transactions are a financial integrity risk on Reserve Bank and FundsLink.

anti_patterns.description: Sequential `prisma.$executeRaw` calls without a transaction wrapper — the first raw write succeeds; the second fails; the database is left in an inconsistent state with no rollback path.

standards.title: Raw SQL Always Parameterised — Never String-Interpolated
standards.statement: All raw SQL queries use parameterised inputs exclusively. `prisma.$queryRaw` uses the tagged template literal form (`Prisma.sql\`...\``) which automatically parameterises. Python raw SQL uses `text(query)` with bound parameters from SQLAlchemy — never f-string or `%`-formatted SQL. String interpolation into SQL is SQL injection — it is forbidden without exception.
standards.rationale: SQL injection is the most common critical web application vulnerability. Parameterised queries are the absolute defence — parameters are never interpreted as SQL syntax regardless of their content. This is not a guideline; it is a security requirement.

anti_patterns.description: `prisma.$queryRawUnsafe(\`SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = '${userId}'\`)` — direct string interpolation into SQL; `userId` can be `' OR '1'='1` and extract the entire table.
`f"SELECT * FROM deposits WHERE user_id = '{user_id}'"` in Python — identical vulnerability pattern in FastAPI.

standards.title: Raw SQL Must Apply Soft Delete Filter — No Implicit Bypass
standards.statement: Raw SQL queries that target soft-deletable tables must include `AND deleted_at IS NULL` (or `WHERE deleted_at IS NULL`) in the WHERE clause. Prisma middleware applies the soft delete filter to ORM queries automatically; raw SQL bypasses this middleware. The filter must be applied manually and explicitly.
standards.rationale: The Prisma soft delete middleware is not invoked for `$queryRaw` or `$executeRaw`. A raw SQL query that omits the soft delete filter will include deleted records silently, producing incorrect aggregate results.

anti_patterns.description: `SELECT SUM(amount) FROM deposits WHERE user_id = $1` without `AND deleted_at IS NULL` — includes soft-deleted deposits in the balance calculation, overstating the user's balance.

standards.title: Raw SQL Results Validated with TypeScript/Pydantic Types
standards.statement: Raw SQL query results in TypeScript are typed using `prisma.$queryRaw<T[]>` with an explicit TypeScript interface for the result shape. Python raw SQL results are validated through a Pydantic model. Raw SQL that returns `any[]` or `dict` without type validation bypasses the type safety that Prisma would otherwise provide.

anti_patterns.description: `const result = await prisma.$queryRaw<any[]>(...)` — the type assertion `any[]` defeats the purpose of TypeScript; schema changes produce runtime errors instead of compile-time errors.

standards.title: Raw SQL Isolated in Dedicated Query Functions — Never Inline in API Routes
standards.statement: Raw SQL queries are isolated in dedicated query functions within the service layer — not inline in API route handlers. Each raw SQL function has a descriptive name (`getStudentFundingMatchAggregates`), type annotations, and the explanatory comment required by S5.19. This makes raw SQL visible, reviewable, and testable in isolation.

anti_patterns.description: Raw SQL written inline in a Next.js API route handler — not discoverable as raw SQL during review, not independently testable, not reusable.

standards.title: Indexes on All Query-Critical Fields
standards.statement: All fields used in WHERE clauses of high-frequency queries have explicit indexes defined in the Prisma schema. Beyond FK fields (S5.13), index candidates include: email (unique index), status fields used in list queries, date fields used in range queries, and any composite index for multi-field query patterns.

anti_patterns.description: `WHERE status = 'ACTIVE' AND created_at > ?` on the Scholarship table without a composite index on `(status, created_at)` — full table scan on every scholarship list query.

standards.title: Never expose `password_hash`, `reset_token`, `refresh_token`, `deleted_at`, or…
standards.statement: Never expose `password_hash`, `reset_token`, `refresh_token`, `deleted_at`, or `internal_notes` fields in any Prisma select query for API responses. These fields are read-only at the database access layer.

standards.title: PostgreSQL enum types for all constrained value sets (status, role, type)
standards.statement: PostgreSQL enum types for all constrained value sets (status, role, type) — string columns for constrained values allow invalid values at the database level.

standards.title: Decimal columns for all monetary values — never `Float`
standards.statement: Decimal columns for all monetary values — never `Float`. `Decimal` preserves precision; `Float` introduces rounding errors on financial calculations.

anti_patterns.description: `Float` column type for monetary values — binary floating point cannot represent most decimal fractions exactly, so the error is present from the first write and compounds across every subsequent calculation.

standards.title: `NOT NULL` constraints on all required fields
standards.statement: `NOT NULL` constraints on all required fields — database-level constraints enforce data integrity independently of application-level validation.

standards.title: `UNIQUE` constraints on fields that must be unique
standards.statement: `UNIQUE` constraints on fields that must be unique — `email`, `cuid` alternate keys, slug fields — enforce at the database level, not only in application code.

standards.title: `CHECK` constraints on business-rule-constrained fields
standards.statement: `CHECK` constraints on business-rule-constrained fields — `amount > 0` for deposits, `interest_rate BETWEEN 0 AND 1` for rates. Database enforces invariants independently of the application.

standards.title: Connection pooling via PgBouncer on Railway
standards.statement: Connection pooling via PgBouncer on Railway — direct database connections from the application are pooled; unbounded direct connections exhaust PostgreSQL's connection limit under load.

standards.title: MongoDB for Document Data Only — Defined Exclusions Apply
standards.statement: MongoDB stores: AI-generated scholarship reasoning, dynamic content with evolving schemas (tags, categories, descriptions), application logs and events, and feature-rich content not requiring cross-table joins. MongoDB never stores: financial transactions, account balances, authentication data, data requiring foreign key constraints, or vector embeddings. These exclusions are absolute.

anti_patterns.description: Using MongoDB for scholarship application status tracking because "it's schemaless" — application status is relational data with foreign key constraints to the User and Scholarship tables; PostgreSQL is correct.

standards.title: Beanie document models include timestamps (`created_at`, `updated_at`) and soft…
standards.statement: Beanie document models include timestamps (`created_at`, `updated_at`) and soft delete (`deleted_at`) on every collection — mirrors the PostgreSQL required fields pattern (S5.10).

standards.title: All Beanie queries include `deleted_at: None` in the filter
standards.statement: All Beanie queries include `deleted_at: None` in the filter — soft delete filter applied explicitly (MongoDB has no middleware equivalent to Prisma's).

standards.title: MongoDB collection names are snake_case and plural
standards.statement: MongoDB collection names are snake_case and plural — `scholarship_contents`, `application_logs`, `ai_reasoning_records`.

standards.title: MongoDB indexes defined in Beanie model class using `Settings.indexes`
standards.statement: MongoDB indexes defined in Beanie model class using `Settings.indexes` — not created ad-hoc or manually in the database.

standards.title: MongoDB documents that reference PostgreSQL entities use `pg_id
standards.statement: MongoDB documents that reference PostgreSQL entities use `pg_id: str` field storing the PostgreSQL `cuid` — per S5.5.

standards.title: Beanie schemas validated with Pydantic v2
standards.statement: Beanie schemas validated with Pydantic v2 — the same validation library used for FastAPI request/response models.

standards.title: Maximum document size awareness
standards.statement: Maximum document size awareness — documents larger than 1MB signal a design problem; split into multiple documents or move to object storage.

standards.title: No transactions spanning PostgreSQL and MongoDB in a single operation
standards.statement: No transactions spanning PostgreSQL and MongoDB in a single operation — if cross-database atomicity is needed, the operation design must be reconsidered.

standards.title: MongoDB connection string in Railway Secrets
standards.statement: MongoDB connection string in Railway Secrets — never committed to version control.

standards.title: MongoDB aggregation pipelines isolated in dedicated service functions with…
standards.statement: MongoDB aggregation pipelines isolated in dedicated service functions with Pydantic result validation — same principle as raw SQL isolation (S5.24).

standards.title: MongoDB write operations always await confirmation
standards.statement: MongoDB write operations always await confirmation — never fire-and-forget writes to MongoDB from the service layer.

standards.title: ChromaDB for Vector Similarity Only — No Structured Data
standards.statement: ChromaDB stores only vector embeddings and their associated semantic metadata (document chunk, source reference, embedding model). Structured data — user IDs, scholarship titles, amounts, dates — lives in PostgreSQL. ChromaDB metadata fields store only the PostgreSQL `cuid` reference needed to retrieve the full document from its authoritative source.

anti_patterns.description: Storing scholarship amounts and eligibility criteria in ChromaDB metadata — duplicates PostgreSQL data; ChromaDB metadata is not the system of record.

standards.title: ChromaDB runs as a separate Railway service with a persistent volume
standards.statement: ChromaDB runs as a separate Railway service with a persistent volume — never co-located with the FastAPI service; volume ensures embedding persistence across restarts.

standards.title: The FastAPI AI service is the only service with write access to ChromaDB
standards.statement: The FastAPI AI service is the only service with write access to ChromaDB — other services are read-only; only the AI embedding pipeline creates or updates embeddings.

standards.title: Similarity threshold minimum 0.7 for matching queries
standards.statement: Similarity threshold minimum 0.7 for matching queries — results below 0.7 cosine similarity are discarded, not returned to the user.

standards.title: ChromaDB collections named by content type and version
standards.statement: ChromaDB collections named by content type and version — `scholarship_embeddings_v1`, `eligibility_documents_v1` — versioning enables migration to a new embedding model without downtime.

standards.title: ChromaDB internal URL only
standards.statement: ChromaDB internal URL only — the ChromaDB Railway service has no public port; only the FastAPI service on the Railway internal network connects to it.

standards.title: Embedding model is locked per collection
standards.statement: Embedding model is locked per collection — changing the embedding model requires a new collection and a re-embedding migration pipeline, not an in-place update.

standards.title: ChromaDB reads in the AI service use `max_results` limits
standards.statement: ChromaDB reads in the AI service use `max_results` limits — unbounded similarity searches are forbidden.

standards.title: Explicit Cross-Database Sync Is Tested
standards.statement: Every operation that writes to multiple databases (PostgreSQL + MongoDB, PostgreSQL + ChromaDB) has an integration test verifying: (1) both writes succeed correctly, and (2) when the second write fails, the first write rolls back or is marked as needing retry. Cross-database sync failures are logged and alerted.

anti_patterns.description: No integration test for the scholarship creation flow that writes to both PostgreSQL and MongoDB — the failure case (PostgreSQL succeeds, MongoDB fails) is untested and produces an orphaned PostgreSQL record.

standards.title: If a PostgreSQL record is soft-deleted, the corresponding MongoDB documents and…
standards.statement: If a PostgreSQL record is soft-deleted, the corresponding MongoDB documents and ChromaDB embeddings are also soft-deleted in the same logical operation — referential integrity is maintained across database types.

standards.title: The cross-database sync operation is idempotent
standards.statement: The cross-database sync operation is idempotent — running it twice produces the same result as running it once; enables safe retry on failure.

standards.title: Cross-database queries (retrieving a MongoDB document and its PostgreSQL…
standards.statement: Cross-database queries (retrieving a MongoDB document and its PostgreSQL entity) are performed as two separate queries joined at the application layer — never attempted through database-level mechanisms.

standards.title: Background jobs that sync data between databases are monitored for failure and…
standards.statement: Background jobs that sync data between databases are monitored for failure and alert on missed runs (per C8 platform reliability standards).

standards.title: A reconciliation script exists for each cross-database relationship that can…
standards.statement: A reconciliation script exists for each cross-database relationship that can detect and report orphaned records — run quarterly or after incidents.

standards.title: Migrations Run Before Service Starts — Migration-First Deploy
standards.statement: Database migrations run as the first step of every production deployment, before the new service version starts. The deployment pipeline is: run `prisma migrate deploy` → health check migration success → deploy new service version. If migration fails, deployment stops and does not proceed. A new service version should never start against an unmigrated schema.
standards.rationale: CF-13 (Common Failure Register): service starts before migration completes, writes occur against old schema, data corruption is possible during the window between service start and migration completion. Migration-first deploy eliminates this window.

standards.title: All migrations are backward-compatible with the previous service version
standards.statement: All migrations are backward-compatible with the previous service version — enables zero-downtime rolling deploys where the old service runs briefly against the new schema.

standards.title: Never delete a column in the same migration that removes it from the code
standards.statement: Never delete a column in the same migration that removes it from the code — deprecate the column first (remove from code, keep in schema), then delete in a subsequent migration after the first migration has deployed successfully.

standards.title: Migration files are never edited after they have been committed
standards.statement: Migration files are never edited after they have been committed — a migration that has been run on any environment is immutable. Create a new migration to correct it.

standards.title: `prisma migrate diff` runs in CI on every PR that changes `schema.prisma`
standards.statement: `prisma migrate diff` runs in CI on every PR that changes `schema.prisma` — detects missing migration files before the PR is merged.

standards.title: Staging migration is performed before production migration
standards.statement: Staging migration is performed before production migration — staging is the validation environment for the migration plan.

standards.title: Ledger Tables Are Immutable — Corrections Are Reversing Entries
enforced_by: Database grants + append-only trigger; reviewed at schema design
standards.statement: Tables that record financial movements — ledgers, financial-event tables, and the audit log — are append-only. The application role holds `INSERT` and `SELECT` only; `UPDATE` and `DELETE` are revoked at the grant layer and additionally blocked by a trigger. A wrong entry is never edited or deleted: it is corrected by a new reversing entry that references the original row. Because soft delete (S5.8) is itself an `UPDATE`, ledger tables are exempt from S5.8 — they permit no mutation at all, not even a `deleted_at` stamp. This standard applies to ledger, financial-event, and audit tables in every KSDRILL system.
standards.rationale: An editable ledger is not a ledger — it is a spreadsheet. Auditability, dispute resolution, and regulatory trust all require that a recorded financial fact can never silently change. Revoking `UPDATE`/`DELETE` at the grant layer stops the application; the trigger stops every path the grant misses (including a mistaken superuser session). Reversing entries preserve the complete, ordered history of what happened and what corrected it. Proven in the FundsLink `schema.sql` by a violation test (`UPDATE`/`DELETE` against the ledger rejected).

anti_patterns.description: `UPDATE` or `DELETE` issued against a ledger, financial-event, or audit table (or a grant that permits it) — the immutable financial record can be silently rewritten; corrections must be reversing entries.

cross_references.description: soft delete — superseded here: ledgers permit no mutation

standards.title: SEO-Critical or Content-Driven Systems Use Next.js
standards.statement: Systems where SEO is a primary requirement — public-facing pages, content-driven platforms, platforms requiring server-side rendering or static generation for discoverability — are assigned to the Next.js stack. The Next.js App Router with SSR/SSG is the correct technical choice for SEO-critical systems; Angular SPA is not.
standards.rationale: Angular is a client-side SPA framework. Without additional SSR infrastructure (Angular Universal), Angular pages are not indexable by search engines. Next.js was built for SSR and SSG — it handles SEO concerns natively without additional configuration.

anti_patterns.description: Building a content-driven, SEO-critical community platform with Angular — the platform is invisible to search engines without complex SSR setup that adds maintenance cost.

standards.title: Enterprise Dashboards or Financial Precision Systems Use Angular+FastAPI
standards.statement: Systems requiring enterprise-grade multi-role dashboards with complex form workflows, precision financial calculations, or AI-powered features requiring a native Python backend are assigned to the Angular+FastAPI stack. Angular's Reactive Forms, strict TypeScript, OnPush change detection, and RxJS composition suit complex enterprise UI. FastAPI's Python runtime enables native LangChain, NumPy, and financial precision libraries.

anti_patterns.description: Building a complex financial calculation system with Next.js JavaScript — JavaScript floating point cannot provide the decimal precision that financial regulation requires; Python's `Decimal` library via FastAPI is the correct tool.

standards.title: Precision Financial Calculations Require FastAPI Python Backend
standards.statement: Any system where financial precision is a core requirement — interest calculations, deposit schedules, currency conversions, balance reconciliation — uses Python FastAPI with the `Decimal` library for all monetary arithmetic. JavaScript `number` floating-point arithmetic is forbidden for financial calculations. This is a hard technical constraint, not a preference.

anti_patterns.description: `0.1 + 0.2` in JavaScript for financial calculations — IEEE 754 floating point produces `0.30000000000000004`; financial systems require exact decimal arithmetic.

standards.title: AI-Powered Features Requiring Python Use Angular+FastAPI
standards.statement: Systems with AI features that natively require Python — LangChain pipelines, RAG implementations, vector similarity via ChromaDB, PyTorch or HuggingFace inference — use the Angular+FastAPI stack. The Python AI ecosystem does not have equivalent JavaScript implementations for production use; using Node.js wrappers introduces fragility and performance overhead.

anti_patterns.description: Implementing a LangChain RAG pipeline via a Node.js wrapper called from Next.js — the wrapper adds network overhead, version mismatch risk, and loses access to the full Python AI ecosystem.

standards.title: Simple Systems May Use Either Stack — ADR Required
standards.statement: Internal tools, admin panels, and simple CRUD systems that do not require SEO, financial precision, or Python AI may use either stack. The decision requires an ADR evaluating: team familiarity, existing infrastructure alignment, expected complexity growth, and maintenance cost. The decision is documented and immutable.

standards.title: Future Systems Require ADR — Rubric Evaluation Mandatory
standards.statement: Every new system — including systems not yet conceived — requires a completed Architecture Decision Record evaluating stack assignment against the rubric criteria (S6.1–S6.5) before development begins. No system starts without a locked ADR and a registered system context file. The ADR is committed to `adrs/` in `governova`.

anti_patterns.description: Starting development on a new system "in the same stack as the last one" without an ADR — the new system's requirements may differ; the assumption is unvalidated.

standards.title: Stack Assignment Is Immutable — No Mid-Build Changes
standards.statement: The stack assignment is locked at ADR creation and immutable for the lifetime of that system's major version. Changing stack mid-build requires: a new ADR superseding the previous, a C6 Major amendment, and written justification for why the original ADR criteria no longer apply. CF-12 documents the consequence of stack changes without this process.

anti_patterns.description: "We'll switch to Next.js because the Angular build is complex" mid-sprint — the complexity is an architectural problem to solve, not a reason to change the stack assignment; a stack change mid-build invalidates all auth, database, and testing decisions made to that point.

standards.title: Every Significant Architectural Decision Requires an ADR
standards.statement: Architecture Decision Records are created for: new system stack assignment, database technology selection for a new data entity class, external service integration (new payment provider, new auth provider, new AI service), and any approved deviation from a constitutional standard. ADRs are stored in `adrs/` in `governova` as `ADR-{NNN}-{short-title}.md`.

anti_patterns.description: Integrating a new external payment API without an ADR — the decision rationale and alternatives considered are lost; the decision appears to be arbitrary to future engineers.

cross_references.description: every new system requires an ADR

standards.title: ADR status values
standards.statement: ADR status values: `proposed` (under review), `accepted` (locked), `superseded` (replaced by newer ADR with reference), `deprecated` (decision no longer applies). An ADR is never deleted — it is superseded or deprecated.

standards.title: ADR template fields
standards.statement: ADR template fields: Title, Date, Status, Context (the forces at play), Decision (what was decided and why), Consequences (what becomes easier and harder), Alternatives Considered (options evaluated and why rejected). All fields are required.

standards.title: Approved constitutional deviations are documented in both the ADR and the…
standards.statement: Approved constitutional deviations are documented in both the ADR and the system context file — the deviation is visible to AI assistants reading the context file before build sessions.

standards.title: Next.js Stack Topology
standards.statement: The Next.js stack is a unified full-stack architecture. Frontend (React, App Router, Tailwind + Custom CSS), API layer (Next.js API Routes under `/api/v1/`), and authentication (NextAuth.js with Prisma Adapter) are co-deployed in one Vercel project. The backend is not a separate server — it is the API route layer within the same deployment. Database: PostgreSQL via Prisma only.

anti_patterns.description: Browser calling a FastAPI backend from a Next.js system — the Next.js stack has no FastAPI; this indicates stack confusion.

standards.title: Angular+FastAPI Stack Topology
standards.statement: The Angular+FastAPI stack is a decoupled enterprise architecture. Frontend (Angular, TypeScript strict, Tailwind + Custom CSS) deploys separately from Backend (FastAPI, Python) on separate platforms. They communicate via authenticated REST. Database: PostgreSQL + MongoDB + Redis (all stacks); ChromaDB (FundsLink only).

anti_patterns.description: Angular component calling Next.js API routes — Angular systems have no Next.js backend; this is a cross-stack confusion indicating incorrect stack assignment.

standards.title: The Two Stacks Never Share Services — No Cross-Stack API Calls
standards.statement: A Next.js system never calls a FastAPI service. An Angular system never calls a Next.js API route. The two stacks are independently complete. Data that needs to flow between systems (future requirement) uses a dedicated integration layer or event bus — never direct cross-stack HTTP calls.
standards.rationale: Cross-stack service calls create coupling between independently deployed systems. A Next.js deployment depending on a Railway FastAPI service creates a single point of failure for the Next.js system that negates the independence of the deployment topology.

anti_patterns.description: Maphophe (Next.js) calling FundsLink's FastAPI endpoint for shared scholarship data — creates a runtime dependency on a separately deployed service; both systems are affected by either system's outage.

standards.title: Each system has exactly one primary API gateway
standards.statement: Each system has exactly one primary API gateway. Next.js systems: `/api/v1/` routes. Angular systems: FastAPI at the Railway internal URL. No secondary API surfaces.

standards.title: Both stacks use the same BullMQ + Redis pattern for background jobs
standards.statement: Both stacks use the same BullMQ + Redis pattern for background jobs — Next.js uses Vercel cron for simple jobs, BullMQ for queue-based workflows. Angular+FastAPI uses Railway Redis with BullMQ for all scheduled and queued operations.

standards.title: Internal service-to-service calls (within the Angular stack
standards.statement: Internal service-to-service calls (within the Angular stack: FastAPI to ChromaDB, FastAPI to MongoDB) use Railway internal networking — never public internet routing for internal traffic.

standards.title: Next.js Authenticated Request Flow
standards.statement:
Every authenticated Next.js request follows this exact flow:

```
1. Browser sends HTTPS request with HttpOnly session cookie
2. Next.js middleware (S3.7) verifies session cookie via NextAuth
3. Session invalid → redirect to /auth/login with callbackUrl
4. Session valid → request proceeds to API route handler
5. API route handler independently verifies session (S3.7 — double layer)
6. Handler extracts user ID and role from session object
7. Service function called with verified user context
8. Service: validate input with Zod (S2.23)
9. Service: authorise (S3.21 — role check) + verify ownership (S3.22)
10. Service: call Prisma ORM or raw SQL (S5.9, S5.19)
11. Service: Prisma includes deleted_at filter (S5.12) + explicit select (S5.11)
12. Service: build response using standard shape (S2.19)
13. API route: return standard JSON response
14. Browser: TanStack Query updates cache; component re-renders
```

anti_patterns.description: Service function performing auth check instead of route handler — auth is a route entry concern per S3.23.

standards.title: Angular+FastAPI Authenticated Request Flow
standards.statement:
Every authenticated Angular+FastAPI request follows this exact flow:

```
1. Angular component calls service method
2. Angular service calls HTTP client
3. HTTP interceptor (S3.15) attaches: Bearer {access_token} + X-Request-ID
4. FastAPI receives request
5. FastAPI Depends(get_current_user): decode RS256 (S3.13) → check JTI deny-list (S3.18) → query User
6. User not found or deleted_at set → 401
7. Depends(require_role(Role)): check role (S3.17)
8. Wrong role → 403
9. Route handler called with authenticated user
10. Service: validate input with Pydantic (S2.23)
11. Service: verify resource ownership (S3.22)
12. Service: Prisma ORM or raw SQL (S5.9, S5.19)
13. Service: build response using Pydantic model (S2.19)
14. FastAPI: return standard JSON
15. Angular interceptor: 401 → trigger silent refresh (S3.15 deduplication)
16. Angular service: update Signal state; component re-renders (S4.30)
```

anti_patterns.description: Access token stored in localStorage — directly violates S3.14; interceptor reads from Angular memory.

standards.title: The `X-Request-ID` header is generated by the interceptor (Angular) or Next.js…
standards.statement: The `X-Request-ID` header is generated by the interceptor (Angular) or Next.js middleware for every request. FastAPI includes it in the structured log entry. Sentry captures it in the frontend error context. This enables full cross-system request tracing (S2.60).

standards.title: Error responses in both stacks use the standard error shape defined in S2.19
standards.statement: Error responses in both stacks use the standard error shape defined in S2.19 — `{ success: false, error: { code, message, details? } }`.

standards.title: API versioning: `/api/v1/` prefix on all routes
standards.statement: API versioning: `/api/v1/` prefix on all routes. When v2 is introduced per S2.76–S2.80, v1 remains live. No request routing changes in the frontend during v1/v2 coexistence.

standards.title: Health check endpoints at `/api/health` (Next.js) and `/health` (FastAPI)…
standards.statement: Health check endpoints at `/api/health` (Next.js) and `/health` (FastAPI) return 200 with database connectivity status. These are the endpoints monitored by Better Stack (S8.10).

standards.title: WebSocket connections (SyncUp real-time features, Reserve Bank live balance)…
standards.statement: WebSocket connections (SyncUp real-time features, Reserve Bank live balance) are managed as separate connection types — they do not go through the standard REST request flow.

standards.title: No Direct Cross-Stack HTTP Calls Between Systems
standards.statement:
Per S6.14 — restated here for emphasis. No system in the Next.js stack calls an endpoint in the Angular+FastAPI stack or vice versa. This is an architectural boundary.

standards.title: Future cross-system data sharing uses a shared PostgreSQL read replica or an…
standards.statement: Future cross-system data sharing uses a shared PostgreSQL read replica or an explicit integration API with its own ADR — never direct service-to-service HTTP calls between stacks.

standards.title: Shared authentication between stacks (a user authenticated in Next.js accessing…
standards.statement: Shared authentication between stacks (a user authenticated in Next.js accessing an Angular system) is not supported in v1. Each system has its own independent auth. Cross-system SSO is a future ADR decision.

standards.title: If business logic requires data from both stacks simultaneously, the feature…
standards.statement: If business logic requires data from both stacks simultaneously, the feature design is incorrect — re-evaluate the feature boundaries per C9 feature governance before implementing.

standards.title: Angular Stack Deploy Order: FastAPI First, Angular Second
standards.statement: When deploying breaking API changes on the Angular stack: (1) Deploy FastAPI to Railway first, wait for health check success. (2) Only if FastAPI deploy succeeds, deploy Angular to Vercel. If FastAPI deploy fails, Angular deploy is skipped — the old Angular version continues calling the old API. This prevents Angular calling API endpoints that don't exist yet.

anti_patterns.description: Deploying Angular before FastAPI when adding new API endpoints — Angular calls the new endpoint before it exists; users see 404 errors until FastAPI deploy completes.

standards.title: Database migration runs before service start on every deployment (S5.59)
standards.statement: Database migration runs before service start on every deployment (S5.59) — this applies to both stacks.

standards.title: Preview deployments for Angular stack PRs that change the API update the…
standards.statement: Preview deployments for Angular stack PRs that change the API update the Railway staging environment — the Angular preview deployment is tested against the staged FastAPI, not against production.

standards.title: Rollback procedure per stack: Next.js
standards.statement: Rollback procedure per stack: Next.js — Vercel one-click rollback to previous deployment. Angular — Vercel rollback for frontend + Railway redeploy previous build for FastAPI + migration rollback if schema changed. Per runbooks.

standards.title: Environment variable changes require coordination
standards.statement: Environment variable changes require coordination — an env var added to FastAPI that Angular reads must be deployed to both Railway Secrets and Vercel environment simultaneously.

| **v1 Done When** | A creator can send a pitch and receive a response through the structured negotiation flow |
| **Databases** | PostgreSQL + Redis (BullMQ for negotiation timers) |
| **ADR** | `adrs/ADR-004-syncup-stack.md` |

standards.title: Brownfield Adoption Is Incremental and Non-Breaking
standards.applies_to: All Stacks · adoption of any existing system
standards.statement: Converting an existing system to Governova compliance is **incremental and non-breaking** — there is no big-bang rewrite. The compliant path is introduced alongside the legacy path (strangler-fig), traffic migrates gradually, and the legacy path is removed only once the new one is proven. Each conversion step is small, behaviour-preserving, individually deployable, and green on all checks before the next begins.
standards.rationale: Big-bang rewrites of running systems are the highest-risk failure mode in adoption: they replace a known-working system with an unproven one in a single step. Incremental, behaviour-preserving migration keeps the system working and reversible at every point.

anti_patterns.description: Rewriting or replacing a working subsystem in one big-bang cutover instead of migrating incrementally behind a strangler boundary.

standards.title: Tests Written Alongside Code — Never After

depends_on.description: feature lifecycle — tests in the same PR

enforced_by: PR review — tests required before approval
standards.statement: Tests are written in the same PR as the feature code they validate. "I'll write tests later" is a constitutional violation. A feature PR without corresponding tests is not approved for merge. The only exception is a pure refactor PR that changes no behaviour and relies on existing test coverage to validate correctness.
standards.rationale: Tests written after a feature are written to match the implementation, not the specification. They verify that the code does what it currently does — which may include the bugs. Tests written alongside a feature are written against the acceptance criteria, which means they catch implementation bugs before merge.

anti_patterns.description: Separate "test tickets" in the sprint for tests to be written after features — tests written in a separate PR have no way to validate the feature against its original acceptance criteria.

cross_references.description: author self-review checklist includes test verification

standards.title: Test Runner Assignment — Locked by Stack, Never Mixed
enforced_by: CI — fails if wrong runner is installed
standards.statement: Test runner assignment is locked by stack. Next.js: Jest + React Testing Library for unit/integration, Playwright for E2E and visual regression. Angular: Vitest + `@analogjs/vitest-angular` for unit/integration, Playwright for E2E. Python/FastAPI: pytest + pytest-asyncio for all backend tests. Installing a non-assigned test runner in a repository is a CI failure.
standards.rationale: Mixed test runner configurations produce inconsistent results, conflicting configuration files, and knowledge fragmentation. The single test runner per context ensures all team members share the same tooling knowledge.

anti_patterns.description: Karma + Jasmine in an Angular project — legacy test runner; Vitest is the assigned runner.
Jest in an Angular project — creates configuration conflicts with Vitest.
Enzyme in a Next.js project — tests implementation details; RTL is the assigned library.

standards.title: Test the Behaviour, Not the Implementation
standards.statement: Tests assert what a function, component, or endpoint does — its outputs, its side effects, its rendered UI — not how it does it. Tests that assert on internal state, private methods, implementation details, or internal component properties break on every refactor. A test suite that requires updating on every refactor is not a safety net — it is a maintenance burden.
standards.rationale: Tests that survive refactors are tests that describe behaviour. "This endpoint returns 200 with a list of scholarships when authenticated" survives a complete service layer rewrite. "This service calls the repository's `findAll` method" does not survive any internal refactor.

anti_patterns.description: `expect(component.isLoading).toBe(false)` on a private property — tests internal state; testing what the user sees (`expect(screen.queryByRole('progressbar')).not.toBeInTheDocument()`) is correct.

cross_references.description: Angular TestBed uses fixture assertions, not internal properties

grounded_in: Sommerville, *Software Engineering* 10e — ch. 8, Software Testing (black-box testing)

standards.title: Tests Are Independent — No Shared Mutable State Between Tests
standards.statement: Each test runs in isolation and produces the same result regardless of execution order. `beforeEach`/`afterEach` reset state between tests. Database tests use transactions that roll back after each test. Shared mutable state between tests is the primary cause of flaky tests.
